question_text: Find c so that f′(c) = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a) for f(x) = x² − 3x − 1, a = −11/7, b = 13/7.

steps.label: Work out the chord slope
steps.margin_note: First mark. Put both values over 49 before subtracting; mixing sevenths and forty-ninths in one line is where the arithmetic usually goes wrong.
steps.memory_tip: b − a = 13/7 + 11/7 = 24/7. Subtracting a negative a is an addition — write that step out.
lines: f is a polynomial, so it is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b).

recall.must_convey: That the chord slope (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a) is computed first and comes to −19/7.

steps.why: The equation in the question IS Lagrange's mean value theorem, written out instead of named — so the paper can ask this same thing either way, and the method does not change. The right-hand side is a plain number, so compute it before touching the derivative.
common_mistakes: Taking b − a as 2/7 by subtracting 11/7 instead of adding it.
Writing 39/7 as 39/49 when putting the terms over a common denominator.

steps.label: Solve f′(c) = the chord slope
steps.margin_note: Second mark. c = 1/7 is the midpoint of [−11/7, 13/7], which is where the point always falls for a quadratic — a quick way to check the arithmetic.
steps.memory_tip: For any quadratic, c is the midpoint of the interval: (−11/7 + 13/7)/2 = 1/7.
lines: −11/7 < 1/7 < 13/7, so c lies inside the interval

recall.must_convey: That 2c − 3 = −19/7 gives c = 1/7, and that 1/7 lies between −11/7 and 13/7.

steps.why: Solving f′(c) = chord slope is the whole content of the mean value theorem. Saying c lies inside (a, b) at the end is the check that the arithmetic is right, since a value outside would contradict the theorem.
common_mistakes: Solving 2c = −19/7 and forgetting to move the −3 across.
Giving c = 2/7 by not dividing by 2 at the last step.
